summary.text: A 53-year-old woman presented with a gradually enlarging anterior neck swelling over two years, more prominent on the right. She had a thyroid procedure in 2008 (approximately 16 years earlier), with unavailable operative records and unknown extent, and thyroid disease in second-degree relatives. She denied symptoms of thyroid dysfunction and compressive symptoms; examination showed a firm non-tender right-predominant multinodular thyroid mass moving with swallowing, no adherence or cervical lymphadenopathy, a negative Pemberton sign and a well-healed lower-neck scar.

Airway assessment and flexible laryngoscopy were normal. Ultrasound showed bilateral thyroid enlargement, a markedly enlarged multinodular right lobe with retrosternal extension and leftward displacement of the trachea. Bilateral FNA yielded benign Bethesda category two cytology. Non-contrast neck CT showed heterogeneous enlargement extending to the thoracic inlet above the brachiocephalic vein confluence without significant vessel compression; the trachea deviated left with mild narrowing but remained patent, with reactive-appearing small bilateral cervical nodes. Twenty-four laboratory values were reported on the day of surgery, including normal thyroid function; PTT was 38.30 seconds versus printed 25–35. Giant recurrent retrosternal multinodular goiter was diagnosed and thyroidectomy scheduled.

Total thyroidectomy removed both lobes and isthmus through a cervical collar approach without sternotomy. Scarring and adhesions were encountered; both recurrent laryngeal nerves were preserved, parathyroids protected and a source-termed paramedian lobe excised. Hemostasis, inferior thyroid vessel control, cervical mobilization and digital blunt dissection allowed upward delivery of the retrosternal portion; a 16 French VAC drain was placed. Estimated blood loss was printed as “approximately 50mm,” an unresolved unit error. Gross specimen weight was approximately 410 g, with right-lobe dimensions 14 × 8.5 cm, left 8.5 × 3.5 × 4 cm, isthmus 2 × 2 cm and a left colloid-filled cyst 6 × 3 × 2.5 cm. The specimen was submitted in 51 tissue blocks, and histology confirmed benign multinodular hyperplasia and degenerative changes, without malignant features. Recovery was uncomplicated, with normal postoperative calcium and no airway obstruction, bleeding or voice change. Undated follow-up documented normal breathing, swallowing and voice, stable serum calcium, a well-healed incision and no nerve-injury signs, hematoma, seroma, wound infection or recurrent swelling. The conclusion’s claim of compressive-symptom resolution does not establish prior symptoms that were explicitly denied.
